skill.title: TypeScript
skill.summary: Narrowing, generics, unions and the limits of compile-time types.
skill.description: Use the type system to make invalid states unrepresentable, and understand exactly what it does and does not guarantee once code is running.

questions.title: `unknown` versus `any`
questions.prompt: Which statement about `unknown` and `any` is correct?

options.text: They are interchangeable; `unknown` is just the newer name
`unknown` must be narrowed before you use it; `any` turns off type checking for that value
`any` is checked at runtime, `unknown` is not

questions.explanation: Any value is assignable to both, but `any` allows every operation without checks and spreads silently through your code. `unknown` allows almost nothing until you narrow it with `typeof`, `instanceof`, a type guard or validation, which makes it the safe type for untrusted data.
rubric: States that `unknown` requires narrowing before use.
States that `any` disables type checking and propagates.
Recommends `unknown` for untrusted input.
misconceptions: TypeScript types are enforced at runtime.

resources.title: TypeScript handbook: More on functions — unknown

questions.acceptance_criteria: States that unknown requires narrowing before use while any disables type checking.

questions.title: Narrowing with `typeof`
questions.prompt: What is the type of `x` on the final `return` line?
questions.explanation: Control-flow analysis removes `string` after the early return inside the `typeof` check, so `x` is `number` on the last line and `toFixed` type-checks.
rubric: Identifies `number` as the narrowed type.
Explains control-flow analysis after an early return.
Names `typeof` as a type guard.
misconceptions: A variable keeps its declared union type throughout the function.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Answers number and attributes it to control-flow narrowing.

questions.title: Indexed access with generics
questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `n`?
questions.explanation: `K` is inferred as the literal type `"name"`, and the indexed access type `T[K]` resolves to `typeof user["name"]`, which is `string`. Constraining `K extends keyof T` also rejects keys that don't exist on `T` at compile time.
rubric: Infers `K` as the literal `"name"`.
Explains the indexed access type `T[K]`.
Notes that the constraint rejects invalid keys.
misconceptions: Generic return types widen to the union of all property types.
Generic functions lose type information and return `any`.

resources.title: TypeScript handbook: Generics — using type parameters in constraints

questions.acceptance_criteria: Answers string and explains indexed access with the inferred literal key.

questions.title: Modelling request state
questions.prompt: A component tracks a request with `{ loading: boolean; data?: User; error?: string }`. Explain what invalid states this allows, then model it with a discriminated union and show how you would guarantee every case is handled when a new state is added.
questions.hint: How many combinations of those three fields are actually meaningful?
questions.explanation: Independent optional fields permit nonsense such as `loading: true` with `data` and `error` both set. A discriminated union (`{ status: "loading" } | { status: "success"; data: User } | { status: "error"; error: string }`) makes those unrepresentable, and `switch (state.status)` narrows each branch. Assigning the remaining value to `never` in the default branch turns a forgotten case into a compile error.
rubric: Lists concrete invalid combinations the original type allows.
Defines a discriminated union with a literal tag field.
Shows narrowing via `switch` or `if` on the tag.
Uses a `never` exhaustiveness check to catch unhandled cases.
misconceptions: Optional fields are enough to model mutually exclusive states.
TypeScript automatically warns about unhandled union members in every `switch`.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Defines a tagged union for the request states and an exhaustiveness check using never.

questions.title: Trusting `as` at an API boundary
questions.prompt: A client does `const user = (await res.json()) as User;`. Explain what this cast does and does not guarantee, describe a realistic failure it hides, and design a safer approach for data crossing the network boundary.
questions.explanation: `as` is a compile-time assertion with no runtime effect; types are erased. If the server changes a field, returns an error body, or a proxy injects HTML, the code continues with wrong data and fails far from the cause. Treat the response as `unknown` and validate it at the boundary with a schema (e.g. Zod or Valibot) or a hand-written type guard, then derive the static type from the schema so the two cannot drift. Decide how failures surface to users.
rubric: States that types are erased and `as` performs no runtime check.
Gives a concrete failure, such as a renamed field or an error payload, and where it would surface.
Proposes runtime validation at the boundary via a schema or type guard.
Explains deriving the TypeScript type from the schema, or generating it from an API contract.
Addresses how validation failures are handled and reported.
misconceptions: If the code compiles, API responses match their declared types.
questions.acceptance_criteria: States that `as` performs no runtime check and proposes runtime validation at the boundary.

questions.title: What does filter return?
questions.prompt: With TypeScript 5.5 or later, what type is inferred for `names`?
questions.code:
const raw: (string | undefined)[] = ["Ada", undefined, "Grace"];
const names = raw.filter((x) => x !== undefined);
questions.hint: What does TypeScript 5.5 infer about the return type of `x => x !== undefined`?
questions.explanation: Since TypeScript 5.5 the compiler infers a type predicate (`x is string`) from simple arrow functions such as `x => x !== undefined`, and `filter` uses that predicate to narrow the result to `string[]`. Earlier versions returned `(string | undefined)[]` unless you wrote the predicate yourself.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “string[]”. Since TypeScript 5.5 the compiler infers a type predicate (`x is string`) from simple arrow functions such as `x => x !== undefined`, and `filter` uses that predicate to narrow the result to `string[]`.
rubric: Gives `string[]` for TypeScript 5.5+.
Explains that the callback is inferred as a type predicate.
Notes the older behaviour or writing an explicit predicate.

resources.title: TypeScript 5.5 release notes: inferred type predicates

questions.title: Fresh literals versus variables
questions.prompt: Which of the two assignments produces a compile error?
questions.hint: Is `extra` a fresh object literal at the point where it is assigned to `u2`?
questions.explanation: TypeScript is structural: an object with extra properties is still assignable to `User`, so line B compiles. Line A is different: excess property checking applies to fresh object literals assigned directly to a typed target, on the assumption that an unknown property there is a typo. This check is a convenience, not a guarantee, and it does not stop extra properties reaching runtime through variables.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Only the line marked A”. TypeScript is structural: an object with extra properties is still assignable to `User`, so line B compiles.
rubric: Identifies line A as the error and line B as allowed.
Explains structural typing for line B.
Explains that excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals.
Notes that types do not strip extra properties at runtime.
misconceptions: Types remove unknown properties at runtime.

resources.title: TypeScript handbook: Object types (excess property checks)

questions.title: An unsound array assignment
questions.prompt: What happens when this code is compiled with `strict` and then run?
questions.hint: Is a `string[]` accepted where a `(string | number)[]` is expected?

options.text: Compiles and runs; `42` is converted to the string `"42"`

questions.explanation: TypeScript treats arrays covariantly: a `string[]` is accepted where `(string | number)[]` is expected, even though the function can push a number into it. This is a known, deliberate unsoundness for convenience. The array then holds `42`, and calling `toUpperCase` on a number throws at runtime. Accept `readonly (string | number)[]` when you only read, or make the function generic so it cannot widen the element type.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Compiles; at runtime `toUpperCase` throws a `TypeError”. TypeScript treats arrays covariantly: a `string[]` is accepted where `(string | number)[]` is expected, even though the function can push a number into it.
rubric: Explains that the code compiles because arrays are treated covariantly.
Identifies the runtime TypeError.
Proposes `readonly` parameters or a generic signature.
misconceptions: The type checker catches every type error.
Mutation through a wider type is always rejected.
